geography.terrain_summary: Fall Line city - sits exactly where the Piedmont's rolling uplands meet the Coastal Plain/Tidewater; James River drops through a 7-mile rapids zone through downtown; avg elevation ~161ft (49m), terrain varies from river-valley floodplain to upland hills to the west/southwest and flatter coastal-plain lowlands east [Tier 2|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.unique_facts: Richmond was Virginia's Revolutionary War-era capital under Governor Thomas Jefferson starting in 1780, and later became the Confederacy's second (and better-known) capital in May 1861 after the seat moved from Montgomery, Alabama, per the American Battlefield Trust [Tier 3|cross_verified:false|estimated|2026-09-18]

geography.disaster_risk: FEMA NRI (independent city): composite ~33.7-36.7 depending on source snapshot, rating 'Very Low' band - both figures fall well within riskbycounty's 0-42.7 Very Low threshold; the adjacent, separate Roanoke County (surrounding suburbs, different jurisdiction) scores notably higher at 52.2 'Relatively Low' - genuine and correctly-distinguished city-vs-county gradient, not a data conflict [Tier 2|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.terrain_summary: Roanoke Valley, within/along the Blue Ridge Mountains; avg elevation ~333m (1,093ft), range 251-680m; mountain-valley setting distinct from the other VA cities in this dataset (all Piedmont/Fall-Line) [Tier 2|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.unique_facts: The Roanoke Star atop Mill Mountain, built in 1949 as a Christmas-shopping marketing stunt, is the world's largest freestanding illuminated man-made star (88.5 ft tall, ~2,000 ft of neon tubing) and is now lit year-round, visible up to 60 miles away on clear nights; it gave Roanoke its 'Star City' nickname, per regional broadcaster WJLA's history coverage [Tier 3|cross_verified:false|estimated|2026-09-18]

geography.disaster_risk: FEMA NRI v1.20: Wicomico County 61st percentile nationally, rating 'Relatively Low' - notably different hazard mix than the Piedmont MD cities: wildfire elevated at 80.9 (highest of any hazard for this county, unusual for the Eastern Shore), flood only 57.8, tornado 33.7 [Tier 2|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.terrain_summary: Delmarva Peninsula/Eastern Shore coastal plain - very low, flat terrain; city elevation only 17-45ft (5-14m); genuinely distinct from every other MD/mid-Atlantic city in this dataset, all of which sit on the Piedmont or Fall Line [Tier 1|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.unique_facts: Despite its inland-feeling location on the Wicomico River, Salisbury is home to the second-largest port in Maryland by tonnage, handling mostly fuel and grain, per Encyclopaedia Britannica's entry on the city [Tier 3|cross_verified:false|estimated|2026-09-18]

geography.disaster_risk: null - no clean current-vintage FEMA NRI composite percentile/rating for Salt Lake County found this pass; independently well-documented that the Wasatch Fault running directly beneath the Salt Lake Valley is the region's dominant seismic hazard (multiple USGS studies of the Wasatch Front earthquake risk specifically), and Salt Lake County has the largest number of wildfire-exposed structures in Utah (138,600 per a First Street Foundation report) - but the exact current composite score/tier needs a follow-up query rather than a guess [Tier 3|cross_verified:false|unverified|2026-09-13]
geography.terrain_summary: Salt Lake Valley, an intermontane valley on the Wasatch Front - bounded by the Wasatch Range (east, peaks to 3,636m) and Oquirrh Mountains (west), with the Great Salt Lake to the northwest; city elevation ~4,327ft (1,319m), valley floor is broad and flat, mountains rise steeply from its edges [Tier 1|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.unique_facts: In 1848 flocks of California gulls reportedly saved Mormon pioneers' second harvest by devouring a crop-destroying infestation of Mormon crickets, an event remembered as the 'Miracle of the Gulls'; the Seagull Monument erected on Temple Square in 1913 is believed to be the first monument dedicated to birds in the US, per the Deseret News [Tier 3|cross_verified:false|estimated|2026-09-18]

geography.disaster_risk: FEMA NRI v1.20: San Diego County composite 100th percentile, 'Very High' - flood 99.7, wildfire maxed at 100 (well-documented wildland-urban interface risk), earthquake 99.7, tornado notably lower at 64.4 [Tier 1|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.terrain_summary: Distinctive mesa-and-canyon topography - flat-topped marine terraces (mesas) dissected by steep east-west canyons (Mission Valley, Rose Canyon, etc.) draining toward the coast; city elevation range -2m to 1,103m (Cowles/Cuyamaca peaks to the east), avg ~125m; creates genuine neighborhood-to-neighborhood microclimates via canyon cold-air pooling [Tier 2|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.unique_facts: San Diego is regarded as the 'birthplace of California': Father Junipero Serra's Mission San Diego de Alcala, dedicated July 16, 1769, was the first of 21 Spanish missions in California and, together with the adjacent Presidio, formed the first permanent European settlement on the US Pacific coast, per the American Historical Association's overview of Spanish California [Tier 3|cross_verified:false|estimated|2026-09-18]

geography.disaster_risk: FEMA NRI v1.20: San Francisco County composite 100th percentile, 'Very High' - notably different hazard profile from the rest of the CA cities in this dataset: earthquake maxed at 99.8 and flood high at 98.6, but wildfire and tornado comparatively low (28.7 and 34.9) given the dense urban, non-wildland-interface setting [Tier 1|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.terrain_summary: Hilly peninsula between the Pacific Ocean and SF Bay - 43 named hills, elevation range 0-282m (Mount Davidson); sits astride the Pacific/North American plate boundary near multiple fault traces (San Andreas along the peninsula, Hayward across the Bay); Marina District built on 1906-earthquake rubble fill, elevated liquefaction risk [Tier 2|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.unique_facts: San Francisco's cable cars, invented by Andrew Smith Hallidie in 1873 after he watched horses struggle on wet, steep cobblestones, survived the 1906 earthquake and fire and were designated the first moving National Historic Landmark in 1964, per the SFMTA and the nonprofit Market Street Railway [Tier 3|cross_verified:true|estimated|2026-09-18]

geography.disaster_risk: FEMA NRI v1.20: Maricopa County composite 100th percentile, 'Very High' - same county reading as Phoenix, no jurisdiction split [Tier 1|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.terrain_summary: Salt River Valley/Sonoran Desert, but with meaningfully more relief than Phoenix proper - city elevation ranges 1,052-4,819ft due to the McDowell Mountains foothills along the city's eastern edge (McDowell Sonoran Preserve, ~30,500 acres); southern Scottsdale near Phoenix is low desert basin, northern/eastern Scottsdale climbs into rugged high-desert terrain [Tier 2|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.unique_facts: Scottsdale adopted 'The West's Most Western Town' as its official motto upon incorporating in 1951, an identity the Chamber of Commerce deliberately cultivated starting in 1947 by giving downtown a Western architectural theme rooted in the area's earlier cattle-ranching history, per the Scottsdale Historical Society [Tier 3|cross_verified:false|estimated|2026-09-18]

geography.disaster_risk: FEMA NRI v1.20: King County composite 100th percentile, 'Very High' - #1 riskiest WA county; earthquake maxed at 99.9-100 (Seattle Fault runs directly beneath the city, plus Cascadia subduction zone exposure), flood also high at 99.5; wildfire/tornado comparatively low (73-80) [Tier 1|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.terrain_summary: Glacially-carved hilly isthmus between Puget Sound and Lake Washington; 'Seven Hills of Seattle' (Capitol Hill, Queen Anne, Beacon Hill, etc.), elevation range 0-158m (West Seattle); Mount Rainier (4,392m stratovolcano) visible ~87km SE; genuine landslide risk on steep glacial-till slopes [Tier 2|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.unique_facts: The Great Seattle Fire of June 6, 1889 (started by an overheated glue pot) destroyed roughly 64 acres of the city's timber core; the post-fire rebuild raised street grades on retaining walls over the old sidewalks, creating the 'Seattle Underground' still toured today, per HistoryLink.org, the state-affiliated online encyclopedia of Washington history [Tier 3|cross_verified:true|estimated|2026-09-18]

geography.disaster_risk: FEMA NRI v1.20: Pierce County composite 98.7 (per direct FEMA hazards.fema.gov report)/99th percentile, 'Relatively High'/'Very High' depending on source rounding - flood 96.2, earthquake 99.6 (Tacoma Fault runs directly through the county, M7.1 scenario modeled by FEMA Region X), landslide and tsunami risk both flagged for Tacoma specifically in FEMA's own regional risk report given its bluff-and-waterfront geography [Tier 1|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.terrain_summary: Rolling hills, steep bluffs, and terraced flat plains rising from Puget Sound to ~440ft (134m) in the city's east; built on a series of terraces overlooking Commencement Bay [Tier 2|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.unique_facts: Tacoma's 'Grit City' nickname began in the late 1990s/early 2000s as an outsider's insult about the city's rough edges, but was reclaimed as a badge of local pride after a 2003 newspaper column reframed 'grit' as authenticity - it's now one of Tacoma's two official nicknames alongside 'City of Destiny,' per locally-founded Grit City Magazine [Tier 3|cross_verified:false|estimated|2026-09-18]

geography.disaster_risk: FEMA NRI: Hillsborough County 99th percentile nationally, 'Relatively High' - top hazards tornado 99.7, flood 97.8, earthquake surprisingly high at 68.5 (regional seismic model artifact, same pattern as Duval County) [Tier 2|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.terrain_summary: Gulf coastal plain around Tampa Bay; flat, low-elevation, similar coastal-plain profile to Miami/Jacksonville but on the Gulf side [Tier 3|cross_verified:false|estimated|2026-09-13] - general coastal-plain inference, not pulled from a dedicated elevation source this pass
geography.unique_facts: Tampa's Gasparilla Pirate Festival, invented in 1904 by a Tampa Tribune editor and local businessman George Hardee for a May Day promotion, is built around the legend of pirate Jose Gaspar - a figure historians say has no documented record in any fleet log or wanted poster - and has since grown into one of the largest parades in the US, per Tampa TV station WFLA [Tier 3|cross_verified:false|estimated|2026-09-18]

geography.disaster_risk: FEMA NRI, Forsyth County: 92nd percentile nationally, rating 'Relatively Moderate' - top hazards flood 94.7, tornado 90.9, earthquake 88.1 [Tier 2|cross_verified:false|single-source|2026-09-13]
geography.terrain_summary: Piedmont region, Piedmont Triad area; rolling hills typical of the region [Tier 2|cross_verified:false|single-source|2026-09-13]
geography.unique_facts: Winston-Salem is a 1913 merger of two adjacent towns - Salem, a Moravian settlement founded in 1766, and Winston, the industrial center R.J. Reynolds built his tobacco empire from starting in 1874 (10,000 workers across 121 buildings by his 1918 death) - joined by a single hyphen, per Our State magazine's history of the city [Tier 3|cross_verified:false|estimated|2026-09-18]

research_target_for.note: New Haven's citywide crime rate runs well above the national average, and the Hill neighborhood around Yale-New Haven Hospital shows above-average violent crime in local data. Swapped to Woodbridge, one of the lowest-crime towns in Connecticut.

geography.disaster_risk: South Central Connecticut Planning Region (CT's current FEMA-equivalent unit, replacing New Haven County): disaster-risk score 4.9/100 on a third-party site's own 0-100 scale - among the lowest in CT, though the broader New Haven County/region has recorded 12 federal disaster declarations since 2000 (mostly hurricanes/tropical storms - Sandy, Irene, Ida - and winter storms), with coastal Milford flagged as the most flood-exposed municipality in the region; VERIFY: same single-source caveat as Farmington - this 4.9 figure is a third-party composite score, not a directly retrieved FEMA NRI percentile [Tier 3|cross_verified:false|single-source|2026-09-13]
geography.terrain_summary: Inland New Haven County, at the headwaters of the Wepawaug River; elevation ~348ft (106m), part of the same general central-CT hilly terrain as Farmington but closer to Long Island Sound; genuinely more inland/elevated than coastal New Haven itself, consistent with the safety-substitute rationale noted in this dataset's residency_context [Tier 1|cross_verified:true|verified|2026-09-13]
geography.unique_facts: In 1661 Woodbridge secretly sheltered three of the 'regicide judges' who had signed the death warrant of England's King Charles I and fled the restored monarchy's pursuit, per the CTHumanities-run Connecticut History project [Tier 3|cross_verified:false|estimated|2026-09-18]
